turns.prompt_text: Could I create a backsquat bar out of steel or wood?

turns.response_html:
Yes, you absolutely can build a squat rack from either steel or wood. Both are valid "maker" projects, but they require very different approaches to tooling and safety design.

Given your background with DIY projects and modeling software, you have the skills to plan this, but your current tooling might make one material significantly more practical than the other.

1. The Wood Route (Most Accessible)

This is the most common DIY approach because 4x4 lumber is forgiving, easy to source, and incredibly strong under vertical compression.

  • The Design: The standard DIY design (often popularized by the "Buff Dudes" plans) uses 4x4 posts for the uprights and 2x4s or 2x6s for bracing. It forms a "power cage" or a half-rack.
  • Tooling: You can build this entirely with a circular saw (or miter saw) and a drill/driver.
  • The "gotcha": Wood is strong vertically (compression) but weak horizontally.
    • Warning: Do not rely on screws alone. Screws have poor shear strength and can snap if you drop a loaded bar. You must use galvanized carriage bolts (1/2" diameter minimum) with washers and nuts for all structural joints.
  • Modeling: Since you have SketchUp, I highly recommend modeling the "bucket" or base dimensions first to ensure it fits your floor space before buying lumber.

2. The Steel Route (Stronger, but Harder to Process)

Steel is permanent and professional, but processing it is difficult without a full fabrication shop.

  • The "No-Weld" Method (Unistrut): You can bolt together a rack using "Strut Channel" (Unistrut/Superstrut) and thick angle brackets. It acts like an industrial erector set. It is extremely strong but can be expensive (fittings cost more than the steel).
  • The Tubing Method: This involves buying 11-gauge 2x2 or 3x3 steel tubing.
    • Tooling Check: Cutting 11-gauge steel is demanding. A compact 3-inch cut-off tool (like an M12) is great for small parts but will struggle with thick structural tubing. You would likely need a dedicated abrasive chop saw or a portaband to get square, safe cuts without burning through dozens of cutting discs.
    • Hole Spacing: Drilling 5/8" or 1" holes perfectly straight through steel tubing for safety pins is very difficult without a drill press.

Wood vs. Steel Comparison

FeatureWood (4x4s)Steel (Tubing/Strut)
CostLow (~$150-$200)High ($300-$500+)
DurabilityGood (indoors), but bulkyExcellent, lifetime usage
ToolingStandard woodworking toolsWelder, Drill Press, or Heavy Chop Saw
SafetyHigh if bolted correctlyVery High
AdjustabilityFixed hole spacing (hard to change)Adjustable (if using Unistrut)

Critical Safety Warning

The most dangerous part of a DIY rack is the safety catch (the bars that catch the weight if you fail a squat).

  • On Wood: People often use 3/4" or 1" black iron plumbing pipe inserted through holes drilled in the 4x4s. Risk: Dropping a heavy bar (300lbs+) can split the wood or bend the pipe.
  • On Steel: You can buy pre-fabricated "J-Cups" and Spotter Arms, but only if you build your rack to standard dimensions (e.g., exactly 2 inches or 3 inches wide). Wood posts (3.5" actual width) usually don't fit standard commercial attachments.

Recommendation

Unless you have access to a heavy-duty drill press and a chop saw, wood is likely the safer and more feasible option for a home build. It allows you to over-engineer the structure with materials you can easily cut and verify.

Would you like me to find a specific set of dimensions for a wooden "bucket" style rack that minimizes footprint?

turns.prompt_text: Yes please, could this be something that I can move outside on a nice day? Assemble/dissassemble with ease
turns.response_html:
Yes, for a setup that you can easily move outside and store away, a full "cage" is impractical. You want Independent Squat Stands.

These are two separate towers (one for the left, one for the right). Because they aren't connected to each other, you can carry them outside one by one.

Here are the two best designs for your specific constraints:

Option 1: The "Bucket" Stand (Easiest & Most Stable)

This is a classic DIY solution. You set 4x4 posts into 5-gallon buckets and fill them with concrete.

  • Why it works: The concrete creates a massive, stable counterweight (approx. 60-80 lbs per foot) that is hard to tip over but easy to move (you just tip the bucket on its edge and roll it like a keg).
  • Mobility: High. No disassembly required; just roll them out.
  • Weather: Excellent. Plastic buckets protect the base; you just need to seal the wood or use pressure-treated lumber.

Rough Build Plan:

  1. Uprights: Two 4x4 posts cut to about 6ft (or 4" lower than your shoulder height).
  2. Base: Two 5-gallon Home Depot/Lowe's buckets.
  3. Anchor: Center the post in the bucket, fill with Quikrete/High-strength concrete. Use a level to ensure it dries perfectly straight.
  4. Racking Point: Screw heavy-duty hooks or build a wood "ledge" on the front of the 4x4s.

Option 2: The "H-Base" Wood Stand (Lighter & Cleaner)

If you don't want to mess with concrete, you build wide wooden feet.

  • Why it works: You use carpentry to create a wide footprint (an "H" or "T" shape) that prevents tipping.
  • Mobility: Very high. Each stand weighs ~25-30 lbs.
  • Storage: They nest together in a corner.

Dimensions for SketchUp: If you model this in SketchUp before cutting, use these dimensions for maximum stability:

  • Uprights: 4x4 lumber. Height = Your shoulder height minus 3 inches.
  • The Foot (Base): 2x4 lumber.
    • Length (Depth): 30 inches minimum (gives you front-to-back stability).
    • Width: 24 inches (gives you side-to-side stability).
  • Bracing: You must add 45-degree supports (gussets) connecting the upright to the base. Use 2x4s or 3/4" plywood triangles.

The "Ease of Assembly" Trick

Since you want to move this easily, do not build a permanent cross-brace connecting the left and right stands. Instead:

  1. Build the two stands completely separate.
  2. To ensure they are spaced correctly every time you set them up outside, cut a single 2x4 to exactly 43 inches (standard rack width).
  3. Lay this "spacer board" on the ground, push your stands against the ends of it, and you are instantly ready to squat with perfect spacing.

Material Recommendation: Pressure Treated Pine

Since this is going outside, buy Pressure Treated (PT) lumber.

  • It resists rot and bugs.
  • Note: It comes wet and heavy. Let it dry in your garage for a week before painting, or it will peel.
  • Fasteners: Use "Hot Dipped Galvanized" or "Exterior Rated" screws/bolts so they don't rust out in the Iowa humidity.

The BOM lists a 10-inch pipe. This is intentional.

  • You will have ~1" sticking out the back.
  • Safety Lock: Place the Hose Clamp on the 1" section sticking out the back of the post. This prevents the pipe from vibrating forward and falling out when you re-rack a heavy squat.

Here is a build plan for "The Sandwich Base" Independent Stands.

This design is superior to the "Bucket" style for you because it lays flat for storage (buckets are bulky) and is easier to carry. The "sandwich" base clamps the uprights securely, preventing the wobble common in cheaper stands.

🛒 The Shopping List (Outdoor Rated)

Since you are in Iowa, humidity and winter storage matter. Buy Pressure Treated (PT) lumber (usually green/brown tint) and Galvanized hardware.

Lumber:

  • 2x — 4x4 x 8 ft (The main uprights)
  • 2x — 2x6 x 8 ft (The heavy base "skis")
  • 1x — 2x4 x 8 ft (Diagonal braces)
  • 1x — 2x4 x 8 ft (The "Spacer" board + spare)

Hardware:

  • 12x — ½" x 6" Galvanized Carriage Bolts (The structural strength)
  • 12x — ½" Washers and Nuts
  • 1 Box — 2 ½" Deck Screws (For tacking things in place before bolting)
  • 2x — ¾" Black Iron Pipe nipples (6 inches long) + 2x End Caps (These are your J-hooks)

🪚 The Cut List

Measure twice, cut once. Wear eye protection.

From the 4x4s (Uprights):

  • Cut both posts to 72 inches (6 ft).
    • Note: If you are taller than 6'2", leave them at 8 ft or cut to 80".
  • Keep the off-cuts! You need them for the base. Cut the remaining 4x4 scrap into four 6-inch blocks.

From the 2x6s (The Base):

  • Cut four pieces at 32 inches long.
    • (These will act as the "skis" on the ground).

From the first 2x4 (Braces):

  • Cut four pieces at roughly 24 inches with 45-degree angles on both ends.
    • (These are the diagonal supports).

From the second 2x4 (The Spacer):

  • Cut one piece exactly 43 inches long.
    • (This is your "setup tool" to ensure the stands are always the perfect width apart).

🔨 Assembly Instructions (Per Stand)

Step 1: Build the Sandwich Base

  1. Lay two 2x6 pieces on their thin edge, parallel to each other.
  2. Place your 4x4 Upright standing vertically in the exact center between them.
  3. Place one 4x4 Block (from your scrap) at the very front between the 2x6s.
  4. Place another 4x4 Block at the very back between the 2x6s.
  5. The Result: You now have a 4x4 post "sandwiched" tightly between two 2x6s, with filler blocks at the ends to make it solid.

Step 2: Bolt it Together (Critical)

  1. Clamp the sandwich tight.
  2. Drill two ½" holes all the way through the 2x6 → 4x4 Upright → 2x6.
  3. Insert Carriage Bolts and tighten hard.
  4. Drill and bolt through the front and back filler blocks as well.

Step 3: Add Braces

  1. Screw your 45-degree 2x4 braces connecting the Upright to the Base. One on the left, one on the right.
  2. Use deck screws here (3-4 per joint); they mostly handle stability, not the bar weight.

Step 4: The Racking Pins (J-Hooks)

  1. Measure your ideal squat rack height.
  2. Drill a ⅞" or 1" hole (depending on pipe outer diameter) straight through the center of the 4x4 upright at that height.
    • Tip: Try to drill this perfectly straight, or your bar will sit crooked.
  3. Insert the Black Iron Pipe. Screw the Cap on the end (this prevents the bar from vibrating off the rack and landing on your toes).

🚜 Outdoor Use & Storage

  • Setup: Carry stands outside. Drop your 43" Spacer Board on the ground. Push the bases of the stands against the ends of the board. You are now perfectly spaced for a standard Olympic barbell.
  • Winter: Because you used galvanized bolts, these can handle some rain, but wood warps. If you store them in a garage/shed, they will last 10+ years.

Sleeping is essentially a 6-to-8-hour static hold. If you spend those hours in a position that reinforces the "open scissors" posture or compresses the rib cage, you will wake up with that "armor" fully locked in place.

Here is how the three main positions affect thoracic rigidity.

1. Stomach Sleeping: The "Neck Wringer"

This is generally the hardest position on the upper back and neck.

  • The Neck Torque: You cannot sleep face down (unless you have a massage table), so you must turn your head 90 degrees to the side. This locks the cervical-thoracic junction (where the neck meets the upper back) in a maximal twist all night.
  • The Pelvic Trap: Gravity pulls your hips deep into the mattress, increasing that Anterior Pelvic Tilt (swayback) we discussed. This forces the "scissors" open and jams the facet joints of the spine together.
  • The Result: You wake up with a stiff lower back and a "kink" in the upper trap area, often requiring that shoulder-raise crack to reset the joint.

2. Side Sleeping: The "Clamshell"

This is the most common position, but it often contributes to scapular instability (that "winging" feeling).

  • The Cave-In: Most people naturally curl into a fetal position. This rounds the upper back (kyphosis), reinforcing the "slump" you might be fighting during the day.
  • The Top Shoulder: Without support, your top arm falls forward across your chest. This drags the shoulder blade away from the spine, putting the Rhomboids and Middle Traps on a constant stretch.
  • Why it matters to you: If you feel the need to "crack" by pulling your shoulder blade back, it’s often because it spent the whole night being dragged forward.
  • The Fix: Hug a pillow. Placing a firm pillow against your chest and draping your top arm over it keeps the shoulder joint stacked and prevents the scapula from drifting forward.

3. Back Sleeping: The "Soldier" (Ideally Best)

Mechanically, this is the most neutral position for the spine, but it requires one specific adjustment to work for you.

  • The Gravity Assist: Lying on your back allows gravity to unroll the shoulders and expand the chest (reversing the "hunch"). The rib cage can move freely (Bucket Handle motion) without being compressed against a mattress.
  • The Trap: If your legs are straight out, your hip flexors (Psoas) might pull your pelvis into that Anterior Tilt. This arches your low back off the mattress and creates tension up the chain.
  • The Fix: Pillow under the knees. This slackens the hip flexors, allowing the pelvis to rock back to neutral and the lower back to settle flat against the bed.

Summary of Sleeping Impacts

PositionEffect on Spine/RibsConnection to "Cracking" Need
StomachTwists neck; jams low back.Creates rotational stiffness at the neck/back junction.
Side (Un-propped)Rounds shoulders; stretches Rhomboids.Top shoulder drift creates the need to "retract and pop" in the morning.
Back (Flat)Can cause lower back arch.May cause "open scissors" tension if knees aren't supported.

The Pillow "fulcrum"

Since you already use a "counter" to extend your spine, you can use your pillow as a passive mobilization tool.

  • Thoracic Extension Night Drill: Before you go to sleep, try lying on your back with a pillow (or a rolled towel) placed horizontally across your back, right at the level of the shoulder blades.
  • Let your head drop back (if comfortable) and arms open to the side.
  • This places the thoracic spine in gentle extension, undoing the day's forward hunch. Even 2 minutes of this can reset the "rigidity" before you sleep.

The position of your pelvis acts as the "foundation" for your spine. Because the spine is a continuous column, if you tilt the foundation, the structure above it must curve in the opposite direction to keep your head level and your eyes on the horizon. This is often called the "Righting Reflex."

Here is how the pelvis creates that "rigidity" you feel in the upper back.

1. The Chain Reaction: The "S" Curve

The most common pattern that leads to upper back tension is Anterior Pelvic Tilt. This is when the front of your pelvis drops forward (imagine pouring water out of the front of a bucket).

  • Step 1 (The Lower Back): When the pelvis tilts forward, your lower back (lumbar spine) is forced into a deep arch. This is called hyper-lordosis.
  • Step 2 (The Compensation): To prevent you from falling backward or staring at the ceiling, your upper back (thoracic spine) must round forward to compensate. This is called hyper-kyphosis.
  • The Result: Your upper back becomes permanently rounded and "stuck" in that position to balance out your lower back. The "rigidity" you feel is the muscles locking down to hold this exaggerated curve.

2. The "Open Scissors" Syndrome

A helpful way to visualize this is the "Open Scissors" analogy.

  • Ideally: Your rib cage and pelvis should be stacked like two cylinders, one directly on top of the other (Closed Scissors). This allows your core muscles to work as a bridge between them.
  • The Dysfunction: When you have an anterior tilt, your pelvis dumps forward and your ribs flare up. The "scissors" open.
    • The Consequence: Your core muscles (abs) get stretched out and turned off. Without the core supporting the spine, your back muscles (the ones you keep cracking) have to work overtime to hold you upright. They become "armored" and rigid because they are doing a job meant for your abs.

3. Why Your "Counter Swim" Feels Good

Your intuitive "counter swim" move is actually correcting this pelvic misalignment:

  1. Leaning Forward: By grabbing the counter and leaning, you often instinctively tuck your tailbone slightly.
  2. Gravity: The weight of your torso pulls the spine straight, temporarily undoing the deep curves caused by the pelvic tilt.
  3. Closing the Scissors: The "swimming" motion forces your rib cage to drop down and connect back with the pelvis, relieving the tension in the back muscles.

A Quick Check: The "Tail Tuck"

To see if your pelvis is the culprit, try this simple reset when you feel the urge to crack your back:

  1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart.
  2. Place one hand on your belly button and one on your lower back.
  3. The Move: Gently tuck your "tail" between your legs (Posterior Tilt). Imagine pulling your belt buckle up toward your nose.
  4. The Check: Notice what happens to your upper back. Usually, as you tuck the pelvis, the upper back naturally straightens up, and the tension drops immediately.

If this relieves the pressure, the "rigidity" isn't a back problem—it's a hip position problem.

The connection between your thoracic spine (upper back) and your breathing is mechanical and direct. In fact, your rib cage and thoracic spine function as a single unit.

If you think of your lungs as balloons, they are encased inside a stiff cage (the ribs). For the balloons to inflate, the cage must expand. The "hinges" that allow the cage to expand are located exactly where you feel that rigidity: the joints where the ribs attach to the spine (the costovertebral and costotransverse joints).

Here is the breakdown of how that rigidity affects your breath, and vice versa.

1. The Mechanics: Pump Handles and Bucket Handles

To take a full breath, your ribs don't just push "out"; they rotate. There are two distinct motions happening in your chest:

  • The Pump Handle (Upper Ribs): The upper ribs (near your collarbone) move like an old-fashioned water pump handle. They lift the sternum (breastbone) up and forward. When your upper back is rounded or rigid, this movement is blocked, making it hard to fill the top of your lungs.
  • The Bucket Handle (Lower Ribs): The lower ribs move like the handle of a bucket being lifted. They swing up and out to the sides, widening your torso.

The Restriction: If the spinal segments are "locked" or rigid, the ribs cannot rotate at their hinges. The bucket handle gets stuck. This physically limits how much air you can take in.

2. The Consequence: "Neck Breathing"

This is likely contributing to the tension you feel in your shoulders.

When your main breathing muscle (the diaphragm) tries to pull air in but the rib cage won't expand because of spinal rigidity, your brain calls for backup. It recruits the "accessory muscles" of respiration.

  • The Culprits: These are the Scalenes (side of neck) and Upper Trapezius (top of shoulders).
  • The Result: Instead of expanding the ribs out, you start pulling the entire rib cage up with your neck muscles 20,000 times a day.
  • The Loop: This causes chronic tightness in the neck and upper shoulders, which leads to more rigidity, which requires more "cracking" to find relief.

3. Breathing as an Internal Wedge

You mentioned "swimming" on the counter to mobilize your spine from the outside. You can also use your breath to mobilize the spine from the inside.

A deep, pressurized breath forces the ribs to rotate against the spine. If you breathe correctly, you are essentially performing an internal stretch against those stiff joints.

Try This: "Crocodile Breathing"

This is a specific drill to force the "Bucket Handle" movement and mobilize the posterior (back) part of the rib cage where you feel the stiffness.

  1. Lie Face Down: Lie on your stomach on the floor. Place your hands on top of each other under your forehead (like a pillow).
  2. Relax: Let your chest sink into the floor.
  3. The Constraint: Because the floor is blocking your belly and chest from expanding forward, the air has to go somewhere else.
  4. The Target: Take a deep breath and try to expand your lower back and side ribs outward.
    • Visualization: Imagine you have gills on your back like a shark, or wings that need to spread apart with every inhale.
  5. The Feedback: You should feel your ribs physically pushing out against your sides and your lower back rising toward the ceiling.

This uses the floor as a tool (similar to your counter pushup) to force the breath into the stiffest parts of your back, gently mobilizing those rigid segments from the inside out.
